title: How We Begin a Novel in Our Classroom
author: Marcus Luther
summary: Marcus Luther uses the opening of his first Frankenstein unit with junior English students to share four priorities for beginning a whole-class novel, drawing on fifteen years of teaching. First, plan the reading calendar deliberately, weighing students' independence, whether the book needs a slow start or momentum, and which moments must be read together. Second, make day one count, which he did with a darkened room, scary music, a two-minute scariest-tiger drawing and a choral reading of Blake, all feeding the unit's question of whether creators are responsible for their creations. Third, find a Goldilocks amount of context by using historical and biographical lenses without sacrificing momentum. Fourth, hold an ungraded reading-habits conversation using an index card of five honest questions instead of a quiz. He argues that the whole-class novel is becoming rare as excerpts and test prep displace books, which makes teaching it well all the more important.
points: Sit down and plan the pacing of a whole-class novel with explicit questions about independence, momentum and in-class versus out-of-class reading.
A memorable first lesson shows that classrooms can be both rigorous and joyful, refusing a false choice between the two.
Limit background context to a historical lens and a biographical lens so that it supports rather than stalls momentum.
Replacing the first reading quiz with an ungraded reading-habits conversation builds trust and reading identity.
Whole-class novels are being displaced by excerpts and test prep, so teachers need support to teach them well.
quotes: To be an English teacher, I think, is to cultivate a culture of this stretching —of helping students not only persevere through the meaningful reading but to shift their own identity as readers.
The way you begin a novel as a classroom matters. It matters a great deal.

The goal of this type of intentional thinking and planning, I think, is not to necessarily arrive at a perfect answer (once again, there isn’t one!) but rather to better understand whatever answer you arrive at with your reading calendar

One of my biggest frustrations is when people imply that the classroom can only be a place where rigorous learning occurs or a place where students are laughing and building community. Consequently, one of my deepest convictions is that we need to refuse that false choice
And spending too much time on background context? A very easy way to forfeit momentum at the most critical stage as you introduce students to the book.
Zero grade attached. Just a conversation. Here’s the cool thing: students were very honest on their index cards.

Something I’m realizing is that if our goal is not just to get students to “read the book” but more importantly to build reading identities that sustain beyond our classroom, we have to make space for conversations around their reading identities
